subject: Dedicated vs Hyperscaler eval - follow-up & next tests
messages:

Subject: Dedicated vs Hyperscaler eval - follow-up & next tests

Hi Sarah (and Raj),

Thanks again for the call this morning — good conversation and helpful context on Acme's latency and capacity needs. Quick recap + proposed next tests so we can make the hyperscaler comparison concrete: 

Recap (from our discussion)
- Goal: evaluate tradeoffs between reserved dedicated capacity (Redwood Dedicated) vs running on hyperscaler GPU endpoints for primary inference (latency-sensitive, production).
- Key success metrics you shared: p95 text-gen latency <= 250ms, sustained throughput of ~200 RPS for the chat endpoint, ability to burst to ~500 RPS for short windows, and predictable unit cost modeling for planning.

High-level differentiators (Redwood Dedicated vs hyperscaler managed endpoints)
- Capacity guarantees: Dedicated = reserved GPU pools + SLA-backed capacity. Hyperscaler = best-effort multi-tenant endpoints; capacity can vary under peak load unless you purchase very large reserved instances with longer lead times.
- Predictable economics: dedicated commits + utilization-based autoscaling yields predictable unit cost vs hyperscaler variable pricing (and egress) under bursty traffic.
- Performance controls: our runtime gives per-route batching/config and KV cache which reduces tokens/latency for repeated prompts. Hyperscalers may need custom infra to match.
- Operational tooling: per-request tracing, token-level cost, rollouts, and automatic fallback to verified smaller model variants for graceful degradation.

Proposed next tests (what would produce apples-to-apples data)
1) Capacity stability test (48hr): sustained 24h window at target throughput (200 RPS) + monitored p95/p99 and cost metrics.
2) Burst test: repeated 5-minute bursts to 500 RPS to observe cold-starts and throttling behavior.
3) Failover test: simulate regional capacity drop and validate automatic routing to fallback pool (measuring failover latency).

Attachments: I’m including a short comparison PDF and a draft test plan (capacity-test-plan.md) — see attachments.

Ask: If that plan looks right, can we kick off a POC next week? Marissa (cc'd) will coordinate POC logistics and procurement items. Also can you confirm the procurement contact + any AWs/contracting constraints up front?

Thanks,
Markus
Markus Klein
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
markus.klein@redwood.inference

Thanks Markus — helpful summary. Two quick clarifications before we lock the POC: 

1) Reserved capacity: when you say "reserved GPU pools + SLA-backed capacity," what does that look like in contractual terms? Are you able to guarantee a minimum number of concurrent slots or a throughput SLA (e.g., 99% of requests served under an X ms p95) or is that operational SLA (uptime/time-to-recover)?

2) Burst capacity mechanics: do bursts consume the reserved capacity pool, or is that separate burst/elastic capacity we pay for on top? How is billing handled during bursts?

Also looping in procurement (procurement@acmecloud.com) — procurement will need a rough cost delta vs our current hyperscaler strategy to evaluate.

—Sarah
Sarah Lee
Head of ML Platform, Acme Cloud

On Tue, Nov 3, 2026 at 4:05 PM Sarah Lee <sarah.lee@acmecloud.com> wrote:
> Thanks Markus — helpful summary. Two quick clarifications before we lock the POC: 
> 
> 1) Reserved capacity: when you say "reserved GPU pools + SLA-backed capacity," what does that look like in contractual terms?

Short answers up front: yes — we offer contract-level capacity commitments (GPU pool size expressed as a number of vGPU slots or target sustained throughput) and measurable SLOs for availability and request success. Contract examples: monthly reserved units with a baseline throughput guarantee (e.g., guaranteed 200 RPS at p95 <= 250ms under standard model profile) + remediation credits if SLOs aren't met. Details are scope/size dependent; we can include specific numbers in the SOW.

2) Burst capacity mechanics: bursts are handled two ways depending on the customer's commitment:
- Option A (preferred): dedicated pool + configured burst buffer. You reserve baseline capacity and buy a smaller burst buffer for short spikes; bursts consume the buffer first, then fallback to routing policies if exceeded. Billing: burst consumption billed at a higher unit rate (transparent line item).
- Option B: reserved baseline only; for additional capacity we route to compatible hosted variants or partner hyperscalers as a configured fallback (billing flows separately).

I've attached the capacity test plan which spells out the exact telemetry we'll collect and expected pass/fail criteria. Proposed POC owner from our side: Marissa Cole (cc).

Proposed concrete next steps:
- Marissa to send a short SOW + procurement worksheet (cost breakouts for baseline vs baseline+burst) — target 48 hours.
- Agree POC start date (we can do Nov 9 if that works for Acme).
- Kickoff call to align endpoints, test dataset, and measurement dashboard.

Let me know if you want the contractual SLO language now or after scope is nailed down.

Regards,
Markus
Attachment: capacity-test-plan.md
